newsitem.title: USA: Gingrich faces growing discontent within party.
newsitem.headline: Gingrich faces growing discontent within party.

text.p: Amid mounting discontent with the leadership of Speaker Newt Gingrich and reports of a thwarted coup, a prominent young conservative on Thursday quit his post on the Republican's House leadership team.
In his resignation, Representative Bill Paxon, 43, of New York cited "a growing crisis of confidence" within the party and the need to "mend its wounds."
The action by one of Gingrich's appointed emissaries to the rank-and-file was only the latest in a series of brush-fire challenges Gingrich has had to stamp out this year.
"I gave you my trust and my word, but since both have been cast in doubt it is clear that I can no longer be an asset to your team in this appointed capacity," Paxon wrote Gingrich.

"Both my word and my relationship with the speaker have been called into question by my involvement in last week's attempt to resolve and heal a growing crisis of confidence within our party's ranks," he said in a separate statement.
Gingrich has been plagued by internal party problems since he narrowly won re-election as speaker in January. He was reprimanded and fined by his colleagues for ethics violations.

In a public display of unity, Gingrich appeared before television cameras at a news conference on taxes flanked by his deputies, House Majority Leader Dick Armey of Texas, Majority Whip Tom DeLay of Texas, Republican Conference Chairman John Boehner of Ohio and newly elected Vice Chairman Jennifer Dunn of Washington.
Asked about the reported plots against him, Gingrich told a reporter, "I'm the speaker. We're winning." But he declined to discuss the implications of Paxon's resignation.

Just one month ago, the party held a lengthy meeting to air disagreements after 50 critics met secretly to discuss dissatisfaction with the leadership's handling of legislation. They denied writing a letter which urged a formal challenge to Gingrich's speakership.

The dispute stemmed from Gingrich's handling of a popular disaster relief bill. The House was forced to give in to President Clinton to avoid a veto but only after they lost the public relations battle with the White House. Several Republicans said they feared the same problems would arise in coming disputes with Clinton over tax and spending bills.

The announcement of Paxon's resignation took lawmakers by surprise. Party sources said it was assumed that Gingrich had asked him to step down after reports surfaced that Paxon had attended a meeting last Thursday in which a move to oust the speaker was discussed.
"People are beginning to put the pieces together and figure out where he was on the continuum of events," a Republican who declined to be named said.
There were signs that the discontent, which had been brewing among conservatives who felt Gingrich had not fought hard enough this year to advance their policies, had spread through the party.

Moderate Republican Representative Marge Roukema of New Jersey told reporters the party needed to clear its troubles. "We better get our act together and fast. We've been elected to do a job. Let's stop this civil war and get to work."
But House Appropriations Committee Chairman Bob Livingston of Louisiana, told reporters Gingrich would emerge stronger. "It is up to us to put Humpty Dumpty together again," he said.

Paxon was first elected to Congress in 1988. He headed the National Republican Congressional Committee and helped engineer the party's recapture of the House in the 1994 elections after 40 years in the minority.

Paxon is married to fellow New York Republican Representative Susan Molinari. She recently announced her resignation from the House to become a CBS weekend television news anchor. She had been the highest ranking Republican woman in the House as vice chairman of the conference.
